question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{-4x-2}$ at the point where $x=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=-4x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln(4),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={4}^{u}\ln(4)\cdot (-4) \\ & =(-4)\cdot {4}^{u}\ln(4) \\ & =-4\cdot {4}^{-4x-2}\ln(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=-1} & =(-4)\cdot {4}^{-4(-1)-2}\ln(4) \\ & =-4\cdot {4}^{2}\ln(4) \\ & =- 64 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=-1$ is $- 64 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=-1$ is

$$
y_1={4}^{2}=16.
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(16)&=(- 64 \ln{\left(4 \right)})\left(x-(-1)\right) \\ y&=- 128 x \ln{\left(2 \right)} - 128 \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 16.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={3}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={3}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={3}^{u}\ln(3),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={3}^{u}\ln(3)\cdot (2) \\ & =(2)\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3) \\ & =2\cdot {3}^{2x+1}\ln(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=0} & =(2)\cdot {3}^{2(0)+1}\ln(3) \\ & =2\cdot {3}^{1}\ln(3) \\ & =6 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is $6 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=0$ is

$$
y_1={3}^{1}=3.
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(3)&=(6 \ln{\left(3 \right)})\left(x-(0)\right) \\ y&=6 x \ln{\left(3 \right)} + 3.\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f={4}^{u},\,u=7x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln4,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =7\cdot {4}^{u}\ln4 \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{u} \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 3\cdot 2^u, \qquad u=1-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 3\cdot 2^u\ln(2),\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{u}\ln(2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{u}\ln(2) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{1-x}\ln(2).\end{aligned}
$$
